pass_a_gloss: (continuing 8.6: and the) Son as some lifeless instrument. 8.7 How, having spat greatly and having set the hands upturned against such savage blasphemies, will one not withdraw, fearing lest he become liable to the divine court even on account of an unchosen hearing? 9. [Chapter title:] About what the heretics say: 'when was the Son begotten and the Spirit proceeded?' and the rest. 9.1 So, there being so many and such clear demonstrations, and the Scripture exhorting 'not to be carried aside by various and strange teachings', and to flee 'the empty talkings', the other-minded, being at a loss to establish the things of their religion from the Scriptures, and (damaged), as though drunk, having their argument on each point tossed here and there, put forward various sophisms composed by them with evil art and much rehearsed, among which are these: 9.2 'are not then all things, he says, from God?' 9.3 To which one must answer: but not begettingly, as the Son, nor processionally, as the Spirit of God, nor is it of such operations, or was it deemed worthy of such admired constitutions. 9.4 Then: 'when then was the Son begotten and the Spirit proceeded?' Then, when the Father was not begotten. For even if from him, yet not after him. 9.5 And as it is unlawful to seek (damaged) in a place, since neither (damaged: is circumscribed) the one who begot and the one begotten, so neither (damaged) in time. 9.6 For the Son being God and Word of the (damaged), but of making. Likewise also the Spirit (damaged). 9.7 And how, he says, was he begotten? This, even if it was written about the Son: 'from the womb before the morning star I begot you', and about the Holy Spirit: 'spirit goes forth from me', and if David sings: 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm and by the spirit of his mouth all their powers', and if Job says: 'divine spirit is the one having made me, and breath of the almighty the one teaching me', and if the Lord teaches: 'the spirit of the truth, which proceeds from the Father', and if Paul writes that it is spirit of God as for men their own, 9.8 nevertheless so surpasses every mind that the same apostle writes to Corinthians: 'and thanks to God, the one always leading us in triumph in Christ and having made manifest through us the smell of the knowledge', as we not having shared in all the knowledge because of its being uncontainable, but as it were of some image or breeze. 9.9 And again: 'and we see through a mirror and in a riddle' the things about him. And very fittingly. 'For glory of the Lord hides a word', according to the divine saying, lying above every created perception by an unspeakable and boundless measure. 9.10 Not because of the unbearable only, but because the before-the-ages and before all creation, if it had not been shown by the Scriptures, was unknown to the creation. 9.11 And again to the same, the second time, on this (damaged: most beautifully): 'but we will not boast into the unmeasured things, but according to the measure of the rule, of which measure God apportioned to us, to reach as far as even you'. And in the first letter he says: 'if anyone thinks he has known something, he has not yet known as he must know'. 9.12 What is the difference of the begetting and of the procession? As the manner is unknown, so also the difference, if indeed it is permitted (page number 4, debris) to hear or speak this very thing; for to assign causes of things above every cause and thought is daring; but to marvel at the divine and to think the fearful notion about it to be fear, is safe. 9.13 'Willing then, he says, did God beget, or not willing?' But we must say beforehand their aim and so answer. 9.14 So the aim is that they make the counter-argument against the guileless from each word. 9.15 For if they grasp 'not willing he begot' (but no one answers this to them), they say: 'then what God does not will he endures, having begotten the Son, a necessity of nature driving him unwilling into this'. 9.16 And if 'willing he begot' is given them, they add: 'then the begetting of the Son hangs from the paternal willing, which provides existence to him in a craftsman's way'. 9.17 But this answer happens to be most senseless. For both the begetting God and Father and 'the radiance of his glory', the Son, come before the willing and the not-willing and every notion; and nothing can be conceived between this one and that one from whom he is. 9.18 And likewise also 'the image of God'. And again the Son is a not beginning nor ceasing existence, first before the willing or not willing. 9.19 So he begot in the nature above counsel and mind. 9.20 But this premise of theirs too is full of absurdity. For a passion of desire goes before the willing, and before the not willing yet making (sentence continues in the next section)
pass_b_english: … Son as a kind of lifeless instrument. How could anyone not spit hard at such savage slanders, hold up his upturned hands against them and withdraw, afraid of being held answerable before the divine court even for a hearing he did not choose?
On what the heretics say: “When was the Son begotten, and when did the Spirit proceed?” and the rest.

There are, then, so many and such clear proofs, and Scripture urges us “not to be carried away by various and strange teachings” (Hebrews 13:9) and to shun “empty talk” (2 Timothy 2:16). Yet the heterodox, at a loss to establish the tenets of their religion from the Scriptures, and [...] like drunken men, with their argument on each point tossed this way and that, put forward various sophisms, put together with evil craft and long rehearsed. Among them are these: “Are not all things, then,” he says, “from God?”

To them we must answer: Yes, but not by begetting, as the Son is, nor by procession, as the Spirit of God is; nor do they share in such operations, nor have they been counted worthy of so glorious a manner of existence.

Next: “When, then, was the Son begotten, and when did the Spirit proceed?” At the time when the Father was not begotten. For though they are from him, they are not after him. And as it is unlawful to seek [...] in a place, since neither the one who begot nor the one begotten is circumscribed [...], so neither [...] in time. For the Son, being God and the Word of the [...], [...] but of making. So too the Spirit [...].

“And how,” he says, “was he begotten?” It is written of the Son, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 110:3), and of the Holy Spirit, “A Spirit goes forth from me”; David sings, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6); Job says, “A divine Spirit is what made me, and the breath of the Almighty is what teaches me” (Job 33:4); the Lord teaches, “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26); and Paul writes that the Spirit is God’s own, as their own spirit is men’s (1 Corinthians 2:11). Yet even so, this so far surpasses every mind that the same Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us has made known the fragrance of the knowledge” (2 Corinthians 2:14). He means that, because it cannot be contained, we have not shared in the whole of the knowledge, but only, as it were, in a kind of semblance or waft of it.

And again: “We see through a mirror and in a riddle” (1 Corinthians 13:12) the things that concern him. And with good reason, for according to the divine saying, “The glory of the Lord hides a word” (Proverbs 25:2), since it lies beyond every created perception by a measure that is unspeakable and boundless. This is not only because it is too heavy to bear, but because what is before the ages and before all creation would have stayed unknown to creation had the Scriptures not made it known.

And again, writing a second time to the same readers, he puts it [...] most beautifully: “But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you” (2 Corinthians 10:13). And in the first letter he says: “If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

What is the difference between begetting and procession? As the manner is unknown, so is the difference, if indeed it is permitted even to hear or to speak of this very thing. For to assign causes to what is beyond all cause and thought is rash; but to marvel at the divine, and to hold that the awesome thought of it is a thing to fear, is safe.

“Did God, then,” he says, “beget willingly or unwillingly?” But we must first state their aim and then answer. Their aim is to turn either word into a counter-argument against simple people. For if they seize on “he begot unwillingly” (though no one gives them that answer), they say: “Then God endured what he did not will when he begot the Son, the necessity of nature driving him to it against his will.” And if they are granted “he begot willingly”, they infer: “So the begetting of the Son hangs on the Father’s will, which gave him existence the way a maker does.”

But such an answer is utterly senseless. For both the God and Father who begot and “the radiance of his glory” (Hebrews 1:3), the Son, come before willing and not willing and before every concept; and nothing can be conceived between the Son and the one from whom he is. The same holds of “the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). Again, the Son is an existence that neither begins nor ends, prior to willing or not willing. So he begot in the nature that is beyond counsel and mind.
But this premise of theirs too is full of absurdity. For a passion of desire goes before willing; and before not willing, yet making …

choices.issue: Draft garbled, reversed and padded with brackets
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. Wrong clauses fixed: 8.7 (‘suffer a great fall … the divine Judge and the hearing of an unappealable grace’ for spitting at the blasphemies and fearing judgment even for an unchosen hearing); 9.1 (‘drinking here and there the word’); 9.3 (‘nor the Spirit by way of procession, according to the Spirit of God’); 9.8 (‘something like a veil’ and a stray ‘carried by a breeze’ for ἰνδάλματος ἢ αὔρας); 9.9 (‘according to the divine explicit’); 9.11 (‘the second [point] is called to this’); 9.12 (‘assign a cause to the Cause’); 9.15 and 9.16 garbled; 9.17 (‘this answer proves unstable’); 9.19 reversed (‘in accordance with will and intellect by nature’ for ‘in the nature that is beyond counsel and mind’); 9.20 (‘not to want is to act’). Seven bracket fillers removed ([he treats], [from Him], [He is], [the Lord], [is ours], [God], [point]) and the archaic ‘unto’. References: ‘(1 Cor 13:12)’ written out; Hebrews 13:9, 2 Timothy 2:16, 1 Corinthians 2:11, Hebrews 1:3, 2 Corinthians 4:4 added. Starts and ends mid-sentence, marked ‘…’.

choices.why: Lacunae and broken words in the copy-text (καὶ ····, ζητεῖν … γὰρ, περιορ…, οὐδ…, το̣ῦ υ̣το, πνεῦμα ., παγκαλο…): legible words translated, gaps marked. περιορ… taken as a form of περιορίζω, ‘circumscribed’; παγκαλο… as παγκάλως, ‘most beautifully’.
Read as δεῖ, the word of 1 Corinthians 8:2; θεῖ is a misprint.

Didymus cites both verses as witness to the Holy Spirit; ‘breath’ would hide his point. πνοή in Job stays ‘breath’.

choices.english: For a passion of desire goes before willing
choices.why: ἡγεῖσθαι with the genitive, ‘go before’; the subject is πάθος, matched in u02-open by ἡ ἐξ ἀνάγκης βία (‘the force of necessity’ before not willing yet making).

choices.english: even for a hearing he did not choose
choices.why: The believer fears guilt merely from having heard the blasphemy against his will.

choices.english: come before … prior to willing or not willing
choices.why: Didymus’ answer to the dilemma: Father and Son precede will and not-will, so the begetting is by nature, not by choice or compulsion.
